name: Kalamian Tagbanwa
confidence_why: Zorc 1977 and his c. 1972 fieldnotes say Kalamian Tagbanwa accent is predictable and Himes 2006 agrees it is not phonemic, but no source states the syllable: the published examples (bálay in Zorc 1977, mátaq in Zorc 1978) are penultimate, Zorc's own notes accent seven of nine listed words on the final syllable (baláy against his published bálay), Ruch's 1959 phoneme chart in Reid 1971 lists stress as a phoneme, and Ruch's 1964 phonology, the only primary description, is unread, so any placement would be a guess.

catalog_quote: [Zorc 1977:244 §10.2.2] "The addition of a neutral suffix (see 4.2.1.) to a base forms a derivative with the same accentual pattern, e.g., PBS *qatúbaŋ + *-an → *qatubáŋan front. In Tg and Bk, the enclitic particles affect the accent in the same way: Tag hindíq not + pa yet → hindi:pá not yet, and Bik daqí + pa → daqipá not yet. Even in languages where the accent falls on a specifiable syllable of every full word, an enclitic changes the accent: Kalamian Tagbanwa bálay house + -u my → balá:yu my house." [Himes 2006:3 §2] "Stress was also phonemic in PPh. Proto-Kalamian (PKlm) seems to have lost stress as a phonemic feature." [Zorc 1978:104 n. 13] "Kalamian [mátaq]" [Zorc fieldnotes, Northern Tagbanwa bundle p. 10, handwritten] "Northern Tagbanwa - some intelligibility with Agutaynon and with Kalamian. Same reflexes as those two, with minor lexical and grammatical differences. ... Stress not phonemic: CV́CCVC automatic" [same bundle p. 6, list headed "Stress"] "ían, bɨlág, mangárɨn, takún; baláy, talagáŋ <x>, tanán, ilə́m, ináy" [same bundle p. 2, "laundry - Northern Tagbanwa" text] "múyaŋ ʔápun manáyaw tuŋ durúŋan ... báklu sabŭnáy yu / báklu kəsəkəsán nu / báklu bənlawán nu / bákluʔ pəyán da / bákluʔ ipakáldaw toŋ sakbáyan ... iulik ku tuŋ bálay / yaka plansaán nu / ipabtaŋ tuŋ aparádur"

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Primary quote CONFIRMED verbatim on the saved page scan (Zorc 1977, PL C-44, p. 244, §10.2.2): "Even in languages where the accent falls on a specifiable syllable of every full word, an enclitic changes the accent: Kalamian Tagbanwa bálay house + -u my → balá:yu my house." Also confirmed on p. 218): "Palawano, Aborlan, and Agutaynen, which also do not have contrastive word accent" (Agutaynen = sister language, not cala1258 itself), and in the text p. 287 n. 8: Zorc gathered Kalamian Tagbanwa data independently and cross-checked it against Reid (1971). Himes 2006:3 §2 CONFIRMED verbatim in lines 74-75: "Stress was also phonemic in PPh. Proto-Kalamian (PKlm) seems to have lost stress as a pho…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive (Himes 2006; Zorc's fieldnote 'Stress not phonemic'); per Zorc 1977 it falls on a predictable ('specifiable') syllable of every full word, which his examples show to be the penult (bálay 'house', [mátaq] 'eye'; closed penult 'CV́CCVC automatic'), and the accent moves rightward so as to stay on the penult of the word-plus-enclitic (bálay + -u → balá:yu 'my house'). No source states the syllable in so many words; 'penult' is inferred from the examples.
new_statements.exceptions: Contradictory data: Reid 1971:42 (Ruch 1959 analysis) lists 'Stress' among the phonemes of Kalamian Tagbanwa; Zorc's own handwritten 'Stress' list (bundle p. 8) marks final stress in baláy, tanán, ináy, takún, bɨlág, talagáŋ, ilə́m beside penult íyan, mangárɨn, and his PPh worksheet has kalawíd, bɨlág; Ruch 1974 omits stress from the phoneme inventory. Zorc 1977:218 says only Palawano, Aborlan and Agutaynen (sister language) lack contrastive word accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word plus enclitic pronoun/particle forms one accentual domain (accent shifts under enclisis, Zorc 1977:244; fieldnote forms kəsəkəsán nu, bənlawán nu). Data are Zorc's field elicitations (Coron, Banwang Daan) cross-checked with Ruch's SIL data; Himes's statement is comparative, based on Reid 1971 / Quakenbush / Ruch data.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data concern Kalamian Tagbanwa proper (= Northern Tagbanwa, Tinagbanwa of Coron Island / Banwang Daan), i.e. cala1258 [tbk]. Zorc's separate 'Kalamian/Kalamyanis' bundle is the Karamiananen (Busuanga/Culion) variety, a coordinate dialect of cala1258 per Himes 2006, elicited from a Kuyonon L1 speaker and not used for the reading. Zorc 1977:218's 'do not have contrastive word accent' names Agutaynen (agut1237, sister language), Palawano and Aborlan, not Kalamian Tagbanwa itself. Himes 2006's statement is about Proto-Kalamian (Agutaynen + Kalamian Tagbanwa dialects).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' (Zorc 1977:244 enclitic-shift example, Himes 2006 'PKlm lost stress as a phonemic feature'): adds the explicit statement that stress is not phonemic, the closed-penult (CV́CCVC) automatic rule, running-text evidence of penult accent in isolation and host-final accent before enclitics, plus an unglossed list of final-accented forms that a cautious entry should flag as unexplained.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not phonemic (predictable). The only rule written is that a CVCCVC word is stressed on its first, closed penultimate syllable automatically. In the connected 'laundry' text (p. 2) words in isolation carry penult accent (múyaŋ, manáyaw, durúŋan, mabubúliŋ, ipakáldaw, sakbáyan, bálay, aparádur), and the accent moves to the final syllable of a host followed by an enclitic pronoun (sabunáy yu, kəsəkəsán nu, bənlawán nu, pəyán da, plansaán nu), the same enclitic shift Zorc 1977:244 reports.
new_statements.exceptions: The pencil list headed 'Stress' on p. 6 has seven final-accented forms (bɨlág, takún, tanán, ilə́m, ináy, baláy, talagáŋ) against two penult forms (ían, mangárɨn); 'baláy' there conflicts with 'bálay' in the p. 2 text and in Zorc 1977:244. Zorc's own conclusion on p. 10 is nonetheless that stress is not phonemic; the list is unglossed and unexplained (a jotted check of candidate contrasts, presumably). Also the nominal negative on p. 10 is written bɨlág with final accent.
new_statements.identity_note: The SEAlang bundle is headed 'Tagbanwa - Northern' and on p. 12 'Kalamian(is) - Tagbanwa (Palawan)'; on p. 10 Zorc distinguishes 'Northern Tagbanwa' (Culion/Coron; Zorc 1977:25 list item 25) from 'Kalamian' (Karamiananen of Busuanga, item 24) as mutually intelligible varieties with the same reflexes. Both fall under cala1258 (Himes 2006:2-3 treats Karamiananen as a coordinate dialect). Earlier readers of this folder record the informant as Rodolfo Aguilar of Coron, Banwang Daan; I did not re-verify that page. Ruch's thesis describes the Coron Island variety.

readall_conflicts: Within Zorc's own fieldnotes: the p. 10 statement 'Stress not phonemic: CV́CCVC automatic' and the p. 2 running text (penult accent on isolated words, accent on the host's final syllable before an enclitic) support predictable penult stress, but the p. 6 pencil list headed 'Stress' gives seven of nine forms with final accent (bɨlág, takún, tanán, ilə́m, ináy, baláy, talagáŋ) and writes baláy where p. 2 and Zorc 1977:244 write bálay. Himes 2006 (already in the catalog) agrees that Proto-Kalamian lost phonemic stress but gives no placement. Ruch 1964, the one primary phonology, could not be opened, so no source yet states a full placement rule for words other than CVCCVC.
